title: Arrays and Strings
summary: Fixed-size arrays, how to find their length, two-dimensional grids, and C strings as char arrays ending in a zero byte, with the string.h functions and safe input.
introduction: An array is a block of elements of one type stored side by side in memory, and a C string is nothing more than an array of `char` that ends with a zero byte. No length is stored anywhere and no check ensures an index is in range, which is why arrays are where C programs most often go wrong. This lesson shows how to declare, initialise and iterate arrays, how to compute their length, how strings work underneath, and which standard functions copy, compare and read them safely.
learningObjectives: Declare, initialise and loop over one- and two-dimensional arrays
Compute an array's element count with sizeof
Explain the null terminator and the difference between strlen and sizeof
Copy, compare and read strings with the safe functions from string.h and stdio.h

blocks.text: `int scores[5];` reserves room for five `int` values numbered 0 to 4. An initialiser list fills them in order; if it is shorter than the array the remaining elements become zero, and if you omit the size the compiler counts the initialisers for you. The index operator `[]` reads or writes one element. Because C stores no length with the array, you track it yourself. The idiom `sizeof scores / sizeof scores[0]` computes the element count of an array that is in scope, since `sizeof` reports the whole array's size in bytes.

blocks.title: scores.c
Terminal
blocks.content:
$ gcc -Wall -Wextra -std=c17 scores.c -o scores
$ ./scores
count = 4
bytes = 16
average = 76.5
60 0

blocks.text: Indexes are of type `size_t`, the unsigned type returned by `sizeof`, which avoids the signed/unsigned warning you would get from comparing an `int` counter with `count`. The `sizeof` trick works only where the array itself is visible; inside a function that receives the array as a parameter it reports the size of a pointer instead, as the [pointers](/tutorials/c/pointers) lesson explains.

An array of arrays gives you a grid. `int grid[3][4]` holds 3 rows of 4 columns, stored row after row in one block of 12 integers. Nested braces initialise it row by row, and nested loops visit every cell.

Terminal
blocks.content:
row 0 sums to 10
row 1 sums to 26
row 2 sums to 42
grid[2][1] = 10

blocks.text: `char name[] = "Ada";` creates an array of **four** bytes: the three letters plus a terminating `'\0'`, the byte with value zero, that marks where the string ends. Every function in `<string.h>` and `<stdio.h>` relies on that terminator. `strlen` counts characters up to it, while `sizeof` reports the whole array including it. A string literal such as `"Ada"` used on its own is read-only memory; writing into it is undefined behaviour, so declare an array whenever you intend to modify text.

Terminal
blocks.content:
strlen = 3, sizeof = 4
last byte is 0
Ada Lovelace (12 chars)
ada Lovelace
1
0

rows: `strlen(s)`
Number of characters before the terminator
Walks the whole string each call; cache it in loops
`strcpy(dst, src)`
Copy `src` into `dst`, terminator included
`dst` must have room for `strlen(src) + 1` bytes
`strcat(dst, src)`
Append `src` to the end of `dst`
Same room requirement, counting the existing content
`strcmp(a, b)`
0 if equal, negative if `a` sorts first, positive otherwise
Never compare strings with `==`; that compares addresses
`strchr(s, c)`
Pointer to the first `c` in `s`, or `NULL`
Check for `NULL` before using the result
`snprintf(buf, n, fmt, ...)`
Format into a buffer of size `n`, always terminated
The safe way to build strings from numbers and text
`strtol(s, &end, 10)`
Parse an integer and report where parsing stopped
Prefer it to `atoi`, which cannot report errors

blocks.text: Never use `gets` (removed from the language in C11) or `scanf("%s")` without a width: both write past the end of the buffer when the input is longer than expected. `fgets(buffer, sizeof buffer, stdin)` reads at most `sizeof buffer - 1` characters and always terminates the string. It keeps the newline when one fits, and `strcspn` finds its position so that one assignment removes it.

blocks.title: greet.c
Terminal (the user typed Grace)
blocks.content:
$ ./greet
Your name? Grace
Hello, Grace! Your name has 5 letters.

blocks.title: Common mistake: forgetting the terminator's byte
blocks.text: `char word[5]; strcpy(word, "hello");` overflows: the five letters need six bytes, and the terminator lands in whatever variable happens to follow `word` in memory. The same off-by-one appears in loops written as `for (i = 0; i <= n; i++)` over an array of `n` elements. Size string buffers as `length + 1`, loop with `<`, and compile with `-fsanitize=address` while developing so the first overrun aborts with a clear report instead of corrupting data silently.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Shrink the `name` buffer in `greet.c` to 6 bytes and type a long name. `fgets` stops after five characters and the program still behaves; the rest of the line stays in the input buffer. Then replace `fgets` with `scanf("%s", name)` and compile with `-fsanitize=address` to watch the sanitizer catch the overflow.

questions.question: How many bytes does `char s[] = "hi";` occupy?
questions.explanation: Two letters plus the terminating zero byte make three bytes. `strlen(s)` is 2, but `sizeof s` is 3.

questions.question: In `int a[3]; a[3] = 1;` the assignment writes to the last element of the array.
questions.explanation: The valid indexes of a three-element array are 0, 1 and 2. Index 3 is one past the end, and writing there is undefined behaviour.
